Chapter Five: Breaking Bad Habits and Navigating Temptation
Forming new habits is just half the story—letting go of the old, unwanted ones is just as crucial.
Why do those bad habits stick around? Well, it's because they give us instant rewards, even if the long-term impact isn't so great. If we can really understand what makes temptation tick—and learn how to handle it—we’ll set ourselves up for real, lasting change.
Temptation is especially tough when it’s right in front of us. Maybe it’s that cookie jar on the kitchen counter, or the constant buzz of your phone. Those triggers can spark automatic behaviors before you even realize it. So, what can you do? The first step is to make those temptations less visible or accessible.
Try removing or hiding the things that pull you in the wrong direction. For example, swap out unhealthy snacks with a bowl of fresh fruit right on your table, so the healthy option is the easiest one to grab.
Or, if you want to cut back on social media, turn off notifications or move the app off your home screen. Basically, you want to add a little friction to your bad habits—make them less convenient, and you’ll do them less often.
There’s another trick called temptation bundling. Imagine letting yourself listen to your favorite podcast, but only while you’re at the gym or out for a walk. Suddenly, that workout doesn’t seem so bad, right? Pairing something you love with something you tend to avoid can make those positive behaviors a lot more tempting.
Scheduling is another game changer. If you set specific times for certain activities—like only checking email at 10 a.m. and 3 p.m.—it’s easier to avoid falling into old habits on a whim. This structure helps you stay focused and keeps distractions in check.
Keeping track of your habits is also huge. When you log when and where you slip up, you start to notice patterns. Maybe stress always leads you to snack, or boredom sends you scrolling through your phone. By spotting these triggers, you can step in and change the script before the habit takes over.
Here are a few ways to monitor your progress:
Write down each time the unwanted behavior pops up, and what you were feeling or doing beforehand. Set reminders or alarms to interrupt those automatic responses, giving yourself a moment to choose differently.
Now, here’s something important—bad habits usually fill some kind of need. Maybe they help you deal with stress, boredom, or just feeling uncomfortable. The key is to find healthier ways to meet those needs.
For instance, if stress eating is your go-to, try taking a short walk or practicing some deep breathing instead. If you catch yourself mindlessly scrolling, maybe pick up a creative hobby, or call a friend to connect. It’s all about swapping out the habit for something that actually makes you feel better in the long run.
And above all, be kind to yourself. Change is rarely a straight path. You’ll have setbacks, and that’s okay—it’s part of the journey. Each lapse is a chance to learn, not a reason to give up. Self-compassion helps you bounce back stronger and keeps you moving forward.
So, here’s the key takeaway: breaking bad habits is all about reducing temptation, putting up a few barriers, and discovering positive alternatives that really work for you. With a mix of practical strategies, some honest self-reflection, and a whole lot of patience, you can let go of habits that don’t serve you and make space for healthier, happier routines.
